did_you_know.text: The Nile was the main source of water and agriculture in ancient Egypt. That makes it a fitting setting for a dream about abundance and famine.
Cattle raising in Egypt was closely connected with the fertile grazing areas near the Nile. The river supported both farming and daily life.
A sheaf or grain ear is the part of the stalk that holds the kernels. This image connects the dream directly to agriculture.
The “east wind” comes from the east, and in Egypt it can bring hot, dry air from the desert. That makes it a fitting image for damaged grain.
The magicians were court experts involved in writing, rituals, and interpreting dreams. They could not give Pharaoh a satisfactory answer.
Joseph’s shaving and change of clothes mark his sudden move from prison to the royal court. Appearance mattered in a formal setting such as Pharaoh’s palace.
Joseph does not present himself as possessing special power; he gives the credit to God. He combines confidence in his ability with humility.
The two dreams present the same idea in two different images. Such repetition emphasizes that the message is important and urgent.
Egypt’s grain harvest depended greatly on the Nile and its yearly flooding. Years of weak floods could lead to severe food shortages.
Many commentators understand “and let him collect a fifth” as setting aside one-fifth of the harvest. This would create a food reserve for difficult years.
Joseph’s plan collects food in cities, near the people who live there. This makes the grain easier to store, manage, and distribute.
A signet ring served as an official signature; its owner could stamp his symbol on documents or soft material. Giving Joseph the ring symbolized great authority.

The meaning of “Avrech” is uncertain, so different translations offer different explanations, such as “bow the knee.” This shows that an ancient word can survive even when its original meaning is unclear.
On, the city connected with Asenath’s father, is usually identified with Heliopolis, an important Egyptian city associated with sun worship. Its Greek name means “city of the sun.”
Joseph is thirty when he receives his position. According to the story, about thirteen years have passed since he was a young man sold into Egypt.
The comparison to the sand of the sea is a vivid expression for an uncountable amount, not a precise measurement. It emphasizes the size of the stores and the abundance collected.
The name Manasseh is connected with the word “made me forget” or “helped me leave behind.” It expresses Joseph’s wish to move beyond the pain of his past.
The name Ephraim is connected with the root meaning “to be fruitful” or “to multiply.” Joseph sees his son’s birth as a sign that he has prospered even in the land where he suffered.
The famine brought people from different lands to Egypt to buy grain. Joseph therefore became more than a local administrator: he gained influence across the region.
